extracted.intended_audience: teachers, students, and readers studying First Amendment / broadcast law (Teaching American History audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and legal standards for evaluating when and how the government may regulate broadcast speech that is indecent but not obscene, as developed in FCC v. Pacifica. Useful for classroom study of constitutional limits on broadcasting and regulatory rationale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content and context are critical elements of First Amendment analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Both the content and the context of speech are critical elements of First Amendment analysis (citing Holmes in Schenck).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court emphasizes that protection depends not just on what is said but on the circumstances in which it is said; evaluators must examine both content and context when deciding if regulation is permissible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear and present danger test (context-sensitive limitation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether words are used in such circumstances and are of such a nature as to create a clear and present danger that they will bring about substantive evils that Congress has a right to prevent (Holmes, Schenck).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Speech may be restricted when it poses a real, context-dependent danger; this principle supports consideration of situational harm rather than categorical protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government may forbid speech calculated to provoke a fight (Chaplinsky / fighting words)
rubrics_metrics.description: The government may forbid speech calculated to provoke a fight (Chaplinsky v. New Hampshire).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fighting-words doctrine is an approved content-based exception; such categories are evaluated according to their tendency to produce immediate harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial speech may be treated differently
rubrics_metrics.description: The government may pay heed to the 'common sense differences between commercial speech and other varieties' (Bates v. State Bar of Arizona).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory analysis distinguishes commercial speech from other speech forms; lower protection may apply to commercial messaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Libel may be treated more severely for private citizens (Gertz)
rubrics_metrics.description: The government may treat libels against private citizens more severely than libels against public officials (Gertz v. Robert Welch, Inc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defamation standards vary with the subject's status; this affects permissible regulation of speech content about private individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obscenity may be wholly prohibited (Miller/Roth line)
rubrics_metrics.description: Obscenity may be wholly prohibited; obscene materials have been denied First Amendment protection because their content is so offensive to contemporary moral standards (Roth; Miller v. California).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obscenity constitutes a distinct unprotected category; application requires assessing community standards and the Miller test where relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadcasting receives more limited First Amendment protection
rubrics_metrics.description: Broadcast media have established a uniquely pervasive presence and have received the most limited First Amendment protection of all forms of communication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justifications include: pervasive presence in Americans' lives, intrusion into the privacy of the home, and unique accessibility to children; these factors support special regulatory treatment of broadcasters that would not apply to print or other media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government may regulate indecent (though not obscene) broadcast speech under a nuisance rationale
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court held that the government may impose limits on broadcast speech that is indecent but not obscene; the Commission’s action rested on a nuisance rationale in which context is all-important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This permits regulation of patently offensive indecent broadcasts in certain contexts without requiring proof of obscenity; the holding is explicitly narrow and context-dependent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual factors for assessing broadcast indecency
rubrics_metrics.description: Context requires consideration of a host of variables: the time of day, the content of the program (which affects audience composition), and differences between radio, television, and closed-circuit transmissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulators should weigh these variables (e.g., whether children are likely to be in the audience at the broadcast time) when determining whether indecent material may be restricted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inability to avoid exposure by listeners (prior warnings insufficient)
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the broadcast audience is constantly tuning in and out, prior warnings cannot completely protect the listener or viewer from unexpected program content; turning off the radio is an inadequate remedy for harm already done.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The practical difficulty of preventing involuntary exposure (including in the home) is a factor justifying regulation of broadcast indecency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government interest in protecting youth and supporting parental authority (Ginsberg)
rubrics_metrics.description: The government’s interest in the 'wellbeing of its youth' and in supporting 'parents’ claim to authority in their own household' justifies the regulation of otherwise protected expression as to children (Ginsberg v. New York).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protection of children and parental authority are legitimate governmental objectives that weigh in favor of time/place/manner restrictions on broadcasts accessible to minors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrowness and limits on the holding (avoid overbreadth)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court emphasizes the narrowness of its holding: it does not decide that occasional expletives in other contexts would justify sanction, nor apply to two-way radio conversations or telecasts of Elizabethan comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory action must be carefully circumscribed and tied to context-specific factors to avoid overbroad censorship of protected speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dissent: voluntary reception reduces government's power; privacy justification limited
rubrics_metrics.description: The dissent argues that an individual's voluntary choice to admit radio communications into the home does not implicate fundamental privacy interests sufficient to justify content regulation, and that public broadcasting is properly viewed as participation in public discourse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under this view, regulators must show that substantial privacy interests are invaded in an intolerable manner before suppressing speech; mere presence of offensive words is not enough.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dissent: presence of children alone insufficient to suppress non-obscene speech; parental prerogatives matter
rubrics_metrics.description: The dissent contends that because the Carlin monologue was not erotic appeal to prurient interests of children, the presence of children does not justify preventing minors from access to non-obscene but controversial materials, and that some parents may prefer such exposure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulation justified solely to protect children must be bounded and cannot override parental rights to make educational or cultural choices for their children without clearer justification.
